reminder: The tangent cone at a point is the zero set of the lowest-degree parts of the variety's equations, taken at that point.
definition: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{A}^n$ be an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) with vanishing [ideal](c:ideal) $I$, and move a point $p\in X$ to the origin. The tangent cone of $X$ at $p$ is the zero set of the initial forms $\mathrm{in}(f)$ of all $f\in I$ (not only of generators), where $\mathrm{in}(f)$ is the lowest-degree nonzero homogeneous part of the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f$.
examples: The node $y^2=x^2(1+x)$ at the origin has initial form $y^2-x^2$, so its tangent cone is the two lines $y=\pm x$.
The cusp $y^2=x^3$ at the origin has initial form $y^2$, so its tangent cone is the line $y=0$ with multiplicity $2$.
At a smooth point the tangent cone is the whole [tangent space](c:tangent-space), a linear space.
Non-example: at the node the Zariski tangent space is the whole plane $\mathbb{A}^2$, but the tangent cone is only the two lines, so the two sets differ.

steps: Let $p$ be a smooth point of $X$ with $\dim X=d$.
Then $I$ holds $n-d$ polynomials with independent linear parts, and these linear parts are their initial forms.
Their common zero set is a $d$-dimensional linear space that contains the tangent cone, and the cone has dimension $d$ too.
So the cone equals this linear space, the tangent space; at a singular point the cone can be non-linear.
links.why: It shows that the tangent cone replaces the tangent space at singular points and agrees with it at smooth points.

reminder: A tensor of type $(r,s)$ on a vector space is a multilinear map that takes $r$ covectors and $s$ vectors to a number.
definition: A tensor of type $(r,s)$ on a finite-dimensional [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over $k$ is an element of the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $V^{\otimes r}\otimes(V^*)^{\otimes s}$, where $V^*$ is the [dual space](c:dual-space). Equivalently, it is a [multilinear map](c:multilinear-map) $(V^*)^r\times V^s\to k$ that is linear in each argument.
examples: A vector is a tensor of type $(1,0)$, and a linear form is a tensor of type $(0,1)$.
An inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a tensor of type $(0,2)$, and a matrix that acts on vectors is a tensor of type $(1,1)$.
The determinant, read as a function of the $n$ columns of an $n\times n$ matrix, is a tensor of type $(0,n)$.
Non-example: the map $(u,v)\mapsto\langle u,v\rangle+1$ is not bilinear, so it is not a tensor of type $(0,2)$.

steps: Take vectors $v_1,\dots,v_r$ in $V$.
Their tensor product $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_r$ lies in $V^{\otimes r}$, so it is a tensor.
A tensor of this form is [decomposable](c:decomposable-tensor); a general tensor is only a finite sum of such tensors.
links.why: It shows that a general tensor is built from decomposable tensors by finite sums.

reminder: The thermodynamic limit lets the number of particles and the volume grow to infinity while the density stays fixed.
definition: For a system of $N$ particles in a region of volume $V$ (its [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure)), the thermodynamic limit is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $N\to\infty$, $V\to\infty$ with the density $N/V$ fixed. One studies quantities per unit volume, such as the free energy density $f=\lim_{V\to\infty}-\frac{1}{\beta V}\log Z$ built from the [partition function](c:partition-function) $Z$, and asks that these limits exist.
examples: In the [Ising model](c:ising-model) on boxes $\{-L,\dots,L\}^d$, the free energy per site converges as $L\to\infty$.
An ideal gas keeps its pressure $P=\rho k_BT$ when $N$ and $V$ grow together with $\rho=N/V$ fixed.
Non-example: letting $N\to\infty$ in a fixed volume $V$ makes the density grow without bound, so it is not a thermodynamic limit.

reminder: The Thompson subgroup $J(P)$ of a finite $p$-group $P$ is the subgroup that its abelian subgroups of largest order generate.
definition: Let $P$ be a finite [p-group](c:p-group). Its Thompson subgroup $J(P)$ is the [subgroup](c:subgroup) generated by all [abelian](c:abelian-group) subgroups of $P$ whose [order](c:order-of-a-group) is the largest possible among the abelian subgroups of $P$.
examples: If $P$ is abelian, then $P$ is its own abelian subgroup of largest order, so $J(P)=P$.
In the dihedral group $D_8$ of order $8$ and in the quaternion group $Q_8$, the abelian subgroups of order $4$ together generate the whole group, so $J(P)=P$.
In the dihedral group of order $16$ only the cyclic subgroup of order $8$ has the largest abelian order, so $J(P)$ is this cyclic group.
Non-example: in the dihedral group of order $16$ a Klein four-subgroup is abelian but has order $4$, not the largest order $8$, so it does not lie in $J(P)$.

reminder: The time complexity of a machine is the largest number of steps that it takes on an input of a given length.
definition: The time complexity of a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M$ that halts on every input is the function $T_M(n)$ equal to the largest number of steps that $M$ takes on an input of length $n$. For a general [algorithm](c:algorithm) one counts the steps of a fixed machine model in the same way, and one usually states only the growth rate, such as $O(n^2)$.
examples: A machine that scans its input once from left to right and halts has time complexity about $n$.
A one-tape machine that decides palindromes by comparing the first and last symbol, then the second and the second to last, and so on, runs in time $O(n^2)$.
Non-example: the number of tape cells that a machine uses is its space complexity, not its time complexity.

reminder: A torsor for a group $G$ is a nonempty set on which $G$ acts freely and transitively.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group). A $G$-torsor is a nonempty [set](c:set) $P$ with a [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ that is [free](c:free-action) and [transitive](c:transitive-action), so for all $x,y\in P$ there is exactly one $g\in G$ with $g\cdot x=y$. A base point $x\in P$ gives a bijection $G\to P$, $g\mapsto g\cdot x$, so $P$ looks like $G$ without a chosen identity.
examples: The group $G$ acting on itself by left multiplication is a $G$-torsor.
An [affine space](c:affine-space) is a torsor for its group of translations: two points differ by exactly one vector.
The solutions of $Ax=b$, when one exists, form a torsor for the additive group $\ker A$.
Non-example: $S_3$ acts on $\{1,2,3\}$ transitively but not freely, so $\{1,2,3\}$ is not an $S_3$-torsor.

steps: Take the group $G$ itself as the set $P$.
Let $G$ act on $P$ by left multiplication $g\cdot x=gx$.
For $x,y\in G$ the only $g$ with $gx=y$ is $yx^{-1}$, so the action is free and transitive.
So $G$ is a torsor for itself, and every torsor with a chosen base point is isomorphic to this one.
links.why: It shows that a torsor with a base point is the group itself, so a torsor only forgets the identity.

steps: Take a principal $G$-bundle $P\to B$.
Let the base $B$ be a single point.
Then $P$ is a set with a free and transitive action of $G$.
So $P$ is a $G$-torsor.
links.why: It shows that a torsor is a principal bundle over a point, and a principal bundle is a family of torsors.

reminder: For a subgroup $H$ of finite index in $G$, the transfer is a homomorphism from $G$ to the abelianization of $H$.
definition: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of finite [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $n$ in a group $G$, and let $t_1,\dots,t_n$ represent the right [cosets](c:coset) $Ht_i$. For $g\in G$ write $t_ig=h_it_{\pi(i)}$ with $h_i\in H$ and $\pi$ a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. The transfer is the [homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $V:G\to H/H'$, $V(g)=h_1h_2\cdots h_nH'$, into the [abelianization](c:abelianization) $H/H'$ of $H$, and it does not depend on the representatives.
examples: If $H$ is central in $G$ and has index $n$, then $V(g)=g^n$ for every $g\in G$.
If $H$ has index $2$ and $g\notin H$, then $V(g)=g^2H'$.
The transfer from $S_3$ to $A_3$ is trivial: it sends a rotation $r$ to $r\cdot r^{-1}=1$ and a transposition $g$ to $g^2=1$.
Non-example: a subgroup of infinite index has no transfer, since the product over all cosets would have infinitely many factors.

reminder: The translation group of dimension $n$ is the space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with vector addition, where $v$ acts as $x\mapsto x+v$.
definition: The translation group of dimension $n$ is the [vector space](c:vector-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ seen as an additive [group](c:group). A vector $v$ stands for the translation $x\mapsto x+v$ of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), and composing the translations by $u$ and $v$ gives the translation by $u+v$.
examples: For $n=1$ it is $(\mathbb{R},+)$: a shift of the line by $a$ followed by a shift by $b$ is a shift by $a+b$.
The translation by $(1,2)$ moves each point of the plane right by $1$ and up by $2$, and its inverse is the translation by $(-1,-2)$.
Non-example: the rotations of the plane about the origin are not translations, since they fix the origin and form a different group.

reminder: A trigonometric series is a series of sines and cosines of integer multiples of $x$ with real coefficients.
definition: A trigonometric series is a [series](c:series) of functions of $x$ of the form $\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n\ge1}(a_n\cos nx+b_n\sin nx)$ with [real](c:real-number) coefficients $a_n,b_n$; in complex form it is $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}c_ne^{inx}$. The coefficients need not come from any function, so a trigonometric series need not be a [Fourier series](c:fourier-series).
examples: The Fourier series of an integrable function $f$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$ is a trigonometric series whose coefficients are integrals of $f$.
The series $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\sin nx}{n}$ is a trigonometric series, and it converges to $(\pi-x)/2$ for $0<x<2\pi$.
A [trigonometric polynomial](c:trigonometric-polynomial) is a trigonometric series with only finitely many nonzero terms.
Non-example: $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\cos(\sqrt{n}\,x)}{n}$ is not a trigonometric series, since the frequencies $\sqrt n$ are not all integers.

steps: Take an integrable function $f$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$.
Compute the coefficients $a_n,b_n$ of $f$ by the usual integrals against $\cos nx$ and $\sin nx$.
The Fourier series of $f$ is the trigonometric series with these coefficients.
The converse fails: a trigonometric series need not have coefficients that come from an integrable function.
links.why: It shows that a Fourier series is the special trigonometric series that comes from a function.

steps: Take a trigonometric polynomial $\sum_{|n|\le N}c_ne^{inx}$.
Set $c_n=0$ for all $|n|>N$.
The result is a trigonometric series with only finitely many nonzero terms.
So every trigonometric polynomial is a trigonometric series, but a series may have infinitely many nonzero terms.
links.why: It shows that a trigonometric series is a trigonometric polynomial without the bound on the frequencies.

reminder: The $n$-truncation of an object is its universal map to an $n$-truncated object, the reflection onto the $n$-truncated objects.
definition: The $n$-truncation of an object $X$ is the reflection of $X$ into the [reflective subcategory](c:reflective-subcategory) of $n$-[truncated objects](c:truncated-object): a map $X\to\tau_{\le n}X$ with $n$-truncated target such that every map from $X$ to an $n$-truncated object factors through it, uniquely up to homotopy. For a space it keeps the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_k$ for $k\le n$ and kills those for $k>n$.
examples: The $0$-truncation of a space $X$ is the set $\pi_0(X)$ of its path components, seen as a discrete space.
The $1$-truncation of a connected pointed space $X$ is the space $K(\pi_1X,1)$.
In homotopy type theory the $(-1)$-truncation of a type $A$ is the proposition that $A$ is inhabited.
Non-example: the identity map of $S^2$ is not a $1$-truncation, since $S^2$ is not $1$-truncated: $\pi_2(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take the full subcategory of $n$-truncated objects of the ambient category.
It is reflective: each object $X$ has a universal map $X\to\tau_{\le n}X$ into it.
The reflector $X\mapsto\tau_{\le n}X$ is the truncation functor.
links.why: It shows that truncation is one instance of reflection, so general facts about reflections apply to it.

reminder: A twisted cohomotopy class of a space is a homotopy class of sections of a bundle of $n$-spheres over that space.
definition: A twist on a space $X$ is a [fibration](c:fibration) $E\to X$ whose fibers are $n$-spheres, for example the unit sphere bundle of a vector bundle of rank $n+1$, which the [J-homomorphism](c:j-homomorphism) produces from the vector bundle. The twisted [cohomotopy](c:cohomotopy) of $X$ in this twist is the set of homotopy classes of [sections](c:section) of $E\to X$.
examples: With the trivial twist $E=X\times S^n$, a section is a map $X\to S^n$, so twisted cohomotopy is the cohomotopy set $[X,S^n]$.
For a vector bundle $V$ of rank $n+1$ with a metric, the classes are homotopy classes of nowhere-zero sections of $V$.
Non-example: homotopy classes of sections of a bundle with torus fibers, not sphere fibers, are not twisted cohomotopy.

steps: Take the trivial twist $E=X\times S^n$ over $X$.
A section of $E\to X$ is the same as a map $X\to S^n$.
Homotopy classes of such sections are the cohomotopy set $[X,S^n]$.
So cohomotopy is twisted cohomotopy with trivial twist, and a nontrivial twist changes the bundle of target spheres.
links.why: It shows that twisted cohomotopy reduces to ordinary cohomotopy when the twist is trivial.

steps: Twisted cohomology in a theory with coefficient space $A$ uses twists that are fibrations with fiber $A$.
Take $A=S^n$, the space that represents cohomotopy.
Then a twisted cohomology class is a homotopy class of sections of the twist.
links.why: It shows that twisted cohomotopy is twisted cohomology with the $n$-sphere as coefficient space.

reminder: A unit distance graph has points of a Euclidean space as vertices and joins two points exactly when their distance is $1$.
definition: The unit distance graph of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has every point of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) as a vertex, and two points are adjacent when their [distance](c:distance) is exactly $1$. A finite unit distance graph is the subgraph that it induces on a finite set of points, so it is a [graph](c:graph) drawn with distinct points as vertices and with edges exactly between the pairs at distance $1$.
examples: Three points at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $1$ give the complete graph $K_3$.
The Moser spindle has $7$ vertices, is a unit distance graph in the plane, and has [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) $4$.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ the four corners of a regular tetrahedron of side $1$ give the complete graph $K_4$.
Non-example: $K_4$ is not a unit distance graph in the plane, because no four points of the plane are all at distance $1$ from each other.

reminder: The unitary group $U(n)$ consists of the complex $n\times n$ matrices whose conjugate transpose is their inverse.
definition: The unitary group $U(n)$ is the [group](c:group) of [isometries](c:isometry) of the complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $\mathbb{C}^n$, that is, of the invertible linear maps that preserve the Hermitian inner product. In coordinates it is the group of $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) $A$ with $A^*A=AA^*=I$, where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose, under matrix product.
examples: $U(1)$ is the group of complex numbers of absolute value $1$, the circle group.
A diagonal matrix with entries $e^{i\theta_1},\dots,e^{i\theta_n}$ and every permutation matrix lie in $U(n)$.
Every real orthogonal matrix lies in $U(n)$.
Non-example: the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible but not unitary, since its columns are not orthonormal.

steps: Take the general linear group $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ of invertible complex matrices.
Fix the Hermitian inner product on $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Keep only the matrices that preserve this inner product.
These matrices form the unitary group, a subgroup of $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$.
links.why: It shows that the unitary group is the part of the general linear group that preserves a Hermitian inner product.

steps: Take a unitary matrix $A$ in $U(n)$.
Its determinant has absolute value $1$.
Add the condition $\det A=1$.
The matrices that meet it form the special unitary group $SU(n)$, a subgroup of $U(n)$.
links.why: It shows which single condition turns the unitary group into the special unitary group.

steps: Take a real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ with $A^TA=I$, that is, an element of $O(n)$.
Its entries are real, so its conjugate transpose is $A^T$.
Hence $A^*A=I$, so $A$ is unitary.
Conversely, a unitary matrix with real entries is orthogonal, so $O(n)=U(n)\cap GL_n(\mathbb{R})$.
links.why: It shows that the orthogonal group is the real case of the unitary group.

reminder: A universal covering space of a space $X$ is a covering space of $X$ whose total space is simply connected.
definition: A universal covering space of a connected, locally path-connected [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [covering space](c:covering-space) $p:\tilde X\to X$ whose total space $\tilde X$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space). When $X$ is also semilocally simply connected it exists and is unique up to isomorphism, and it covers every other connected covering of $X$, which is its [universal property](c:universal-property).
examples: The map $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$, is the universal covering space of the circle.
The map $\mathbb{R}^n\to T^n=(S^1)^n$ is the universal covering space of the torus.
For $n\ge2$ the quotient map $S^n\to\mathbb{RP}^n$ is a universal covering space with two sheets.
Non-example: the squaring map $S^1\to S^1$, $z\mapsto z^2$, is a covering, but its total space is not simply connected.

steps: Take a covering space $p:Y\to X$ with $Y$ connected.
Add the condition that $Y$ is simply connected, that is, $\pi_1(Y)=1$.
Under this condition, every connected covering of $X$ is itself covered by $Y$.
links.why: It shows that the universal covering sits at the top of all connected coverings of $X$.

reminder: The upper central series is the chain $1=Z_0\le Z_1\le\cdots$ where $Z_{i+1}/Z_i$ is the center of $G/Z_i$.
definition: The upper central series of a [group](c:group) $G$ is the chain of subgroups $1=Z_0\le Z_1\le Z_2\le\cdots$ in which $Z_1$ is the [center](c:center) of $G$ and $Z_{i+1}$ is the preimage in $G$ of the center of $G/Z_i$. The series reaches $G$ exactly when $G$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-group).
examples: For an abelian group $G$ we have $Z_1=G$, so the series is $1\le G$.
For the dihedral group $D_8$ of order $8$ we have $Z_1=\{1,r^2\}$ and $Z_2=D_8$.
For $S_3$ the center is trivial, so $Z_i=1$ for all $i$ and the series never reaches $S_3$.
Non-example: the lower central series $G\ge[G,G]\ge\cdots$ is not the upper central series, since it descends and uses commutator subgroups instead of centers.

reminder: Upper numbering relabels the ramification groups of a Galois group so that the labels stay the same when one passes to quotients.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a finite [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) of [local fields](c:local-field) with [Galois group](c:galois-group) $G$ and lower [ramification groups](c:ramification-group) $G_u=G_{\lceil u\rceil}$ for real $u\ge-1$. The upper numbering is $G^v=G_{\psi(v)}$, where $\psi$ is the inverse of the Herbrand function $\varphi(u)=\int_0^u\frac{dt}{[G_0:G_t]}$. It is compatible with quotients: $(G/H)^v=G^vH/H$ for every normal subgroup $H$ of $G$.
examples: If $L/K$ is tamely ramified, then $G^0=G_0$ is the inertia group and $G^v=1$ for $v>0$.
For $\mathbb{Q}_p(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}_p$ the group $G$ is cyclic of order $p-1$, with $G^0=G$ and $G^v=1$ for $v>0$.
For a totally ramified cyclic extension of degree $p$ with its only lower jump at $i$, the upper jump is also at $i$, since $G_0=G$ gives $\varphi(u)=u$ for $u\le i$.
Non-example: the lower numbering $G_i$ is compatible with subgroups, $H_i=G_i\cap H$, but not with quotients, so it is not the upper numbering.

reminder: A Vassiliev invariant of order $n$ is a knot invariant that vanishes on singular knots with more than $n$ double points.
definition: Extend a [knot invariant](c:knot-invariant) $v$ to [singular knots](c:singular-knot), which are immersed [knots](c:knot) with finitely many transversal double points, by the rule $v(K_\times)=v(K_+)-v(K_-)$, where $K_+$ and $K_-$ resolve the double point of $K_\times$ with a positive and a negative crossing. The invariant $v$ is a Vassiliev invariant (or finite type invariant) of order at most $n$ when its extension is zero on every singular knot with more than $n$ double points.
examples: Every constant function is a Vassiliev invariant of order $0$.
The coefficient $c_2$ of the Conway polynomial is a Vassiliev invariant of order $2$.
After the substitution $t=e^h$, the coefficient of $h^n$ in the Jones polynomial is a Vassiliev invariant of order at most $n$.
Non-example: the writhe of a diagram changes under the first Reidemeister move, so it is not a knot invariant and hence not a Vassiliev invariant.

steps: Take a knot invariant $v$, a function that is constant on isotopy classes of knots.
Extend $v$ to singular knots by the rule $v(K_\times)=v(K_+)-v(K_-)$.
Add the condition that the extension vanishes on all singular knots with more than $n$ double points.
links.why: It shows that the finiteness condition is the only extra requirement over an arbitrary knot invariant.

reminder: A vertex operator algebra is a graded vector space with a vacuum, a conformal vector and fields $Y(a,z)$ that obey locality.
definition: A vertex operator algebra is a [graded vector space](c:graded-vector-space) $V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}V_n$ with $\dim V_n<\infty$ and $V_n=0$ for $n\ll0$, together with a vacuum vector $\mathbf 1\in V_0$ and a conformal vector $\omega\in V_2$. Each $a\in V$ gives a field $Y(a,z)=\sum_na_{(n)}z^{-n-1}$, a [formal series](c:formal-power-series) of operators on $V$ such that $Y(a,z)b$ has only finitely many negative powers of $z$, $Y(\mathbf 1,z)=\mathrm{id}_V$, $Y(a,z)\mathbf 1|_{z=0}=a$ and $Y(L_{-1}a,z)=\partial_zY(a,z)$. The fields are mutually local, $(z-w)^N[Y(a,z),Y(b,w)]=0$ for $N\gg0$, and the modes $L_n$ of $Y(\omega,z)$ give an action of the [Virasoro algebra](c:virasoro-algebra) with $L_0$ acting as $n$ on $V_n$.
examples: The Heisenberg vertex operator algebra, the Fock space of one free boson, has central charge $1$.
The lattice vertex operator algebra $V_L$ of a positive definite even lattice $L$ is a vertex operator algebra.
The moonshine module $V^\natural$ has central charge $24$, and its automorphism group is the Monster.
Non-example: an associative algebra with only a product has no fields $Y(a,z)$, no grading by $L_0$ and no conformal vector, so it is not a vertex operator algebra.

steps: Take a super vertex operator algebra $V=V_{\bar 0}\oplus V_{\bar 1}$ with an even part and an odd part.
Assume that the odd part $V_{\bar 1}$ is zero.
Then all fields are even, and locality is the ordinary commutator condition.
So $V$ is a vertex operator algebra.
links.why: It shows that vertex operator algebras are the purely even case of the super version.

reminder: Vertical composition joins $\alpha:f\Rightarrow g$ and $\beta:g\Rightarrow h$, two 2-morphisms between parallel 1-morphisms, into $\beta\cdot\alpha:f\Rightarrow h$.
definition: In a [2-category](c:2-category), let $f,g,h:A\to B$ be parallel [1-morphisms](c:1-morphism) and let $\alpha:f\Rightarrow g$ and $\beta:g\Rightarrow h$ be [2-morphisms](c:2-morphism). Their vertical composite is the 2-morphism $\beta\cdot\alpha:f\Rightarrow h$; this operation is associative and has the identity 2-morphisms $\mathrm{id}_f$ as units, so the 1-morphisms $A\to B$ and the 2-morphisms between them form a category.
examples: In the 2-category of categories, functors and natural transformations, $(\beta\cdot\alpha)_x=\beta_x\circ\alpha_x$ for $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$ and $\beta:G\Rightarrow H$.
Draw $\alpha$ as a 2-cell from $f$ to $g$ and $\beta$ as a 2-cell from $g$ to $h$; stacking them along $g$ gives $\beta\cdot\alpha$.

Non-example: [horizontal composition](c:horizontal-composition) combines $\alpha:f\Rightarrow f'$ and $\beta:g\Rightarrow g'$ with $f,f':A\to B$ and $g,g':B\to C$, and gives $gf\Rightarrow g'f'$, so it is not vertical.

steps: Fix objects $A$ and $B$ of the 2-category.
Take the 1-morphisms $A\to B$ as objects and the 2-morphisms between them as morphisms.
These form a category, the [hom-category](c:hom-category), whose composition is vertical composition.
So vertical composition is ordinary composition of morphisms in this category.
links.why: It shows that vertical composition obeys the same associativity and unit laws as ordinary composition.

reminder: The wave equation sets the Laplace operator of a pseudo-Riemannian metric, applied to a function, equal to zero.
definition: On a [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold) $(X,g)$ with [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator) $\Box$ (the Laplace-Beltrami operator of $g$), the wave equation for a function $\psi$ on $X$ is the [linear differential equation](c:linear-differential-equation) $\Box\psi=0$. On Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^{1,n}$ with speed of light $1$ it reads $\partial_t^2\psi=\Delta\psi$, where $\Delta$ is the spatial Laplacian.
examples: In one space dimension every solution has the form $\psi(t,x)=F(x-t)+G(x+t)$, a sum of two traveling waves.
A plane wave $\psi=e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}$ solves the equation exactly when $\omega^2=|k|^2$.
Non-example: the [heat equation](c:heat-equation) $\partial_tu=\Delta u$ is first order in time, and its solutions diffuse instead of traveling at finite speed.

steps: Take the Klein-Gordon equation, which adds a mass term $m^2\psi$ to $\Box\psi$.
Set the mass $m$ to $0$.
The mass term vanishes and the equation becomes $\Box\psi=0$, the wave equation.
links.why: It shows that the wave equation is the massless Klein-Gordon equation, so results for Klein-Gordon apply to it.

steps: Write $\Box$ in coordinates as a second-order linear differential operator with smooth coefficients.
Then $\Box\psi=0$ is a homogeneous linear equation in $\psi$.
So sums and scalar multiples of solutions are solutions again.
links.why: It shows that solutions of the wave equation obey the superposition principle.

reminder: The WZW model is a sigma-model on a surface with a Lie group as target and a Wess-Zumino term of level $k$.
definition: For a compact Lie group $G$ and an integer $k$ (the level), the WZW model is the 2-dimensional [sigma-model](c:sigma-model) of maps $g:\Sigma\to G$ from a surface $\Sigma$ to the [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$, with action equal to the kinetic term plus $k$ times the Wess-Zumino term. The Wess-Zumino term is the integral of the pullback of the canonical bi-invariant 3-form of $G$ over a 3-manifold with boundary $\Sigma$ to which $g$ extends. The model is a [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory) whose symmetry is a [current algebra](c:current-algebra), two commuting copies of the affine Lie algebra of $G$ at level $k$.
examples: The model for $G=SU(2)$ at level $k$ has [central charge](c:central-charge) $3k/(k+2)$.
The $SU(2)$ model at level $1$ is the free compact boson at the self-dual radius.
Non-example: the principal chiral model on a simple group has no Wess-Zumino term, and it is not conformal at the quantum level.

steps: Take the target space of a sigma-model to be a compact Lie group $G$.
Add to the action the Wess-Zumino term, which comes from the closed bi-invariant 3-form of $G$.
Choose the level $k$ so that $k$ times this 3-form has integral periods, which makes the action well defined.
The resulting sigma-model is the WZW model.
links.why: It shows what the WZW model adds to a plain sigma-model: a Lie group target and a quantized Wess-Zumino term.

reminder: A Whittaker function is the solution of Whittaker's equation that behaves like $e^{-z/2}z^{\kappa}$ as $z\to+\infty$.
definition: The Whittaker functions $W_{\kappa,\mu}(z)$ solve Whittaker's [differential equation](c:differential-equation) $w''+\left(-\frac14+\frac{\kappa}{z}+\frac{1/4-\mu^2}{z^2}\right)w=0$, and $W_{\kappa,\mu}$ is the solution with $W_{\kappa,\mu}(z)\sim e^{-z/2}z^{\kappa}$ as $z\to+\infty$. In terms of Tricomi's confluent hypergeometric function $U$, $W_{\kappa,\mu}(z)=e^{-z/2}z^{\mu+1/2}U(\tfrac12+\mu-\kappa,1+2\mu,z)$. In representation theory the same name is also given to functions $f$ on a [group](c:group) with $f(ng)=\psi(n)f(g)$ for a unipotent subgroup $N$ and a character $\psi$ of $N$.
examples: $W_{0,\mu}(z)=\sqrt{z/\pi}\,K_\mu(z/2)$, where $K_\mu$ is a modified [Bessel function](c:bessel-function).
For $\kappa=\mu+\frac12$ we have $U(0,b,z)=1$, so $W_{\kappa,\mu}(z)=e^{-z/2}z^{\mu+1/2}$.
Non-example: the other standard solution $M_{\kappa,\mu}(z)$ of the same equation grows like $e^{z/2}$ for most parameters, so it is not a Whittaker function $W_{\kappa,\mu}$.

reminder: A Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ is a filling of the boxes of the Young diagram of $\lambda$ with positive integers.
definition: Let $\lambda=(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k>0)$ be an [integer partition](c:integer-partition), and let its [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) have $k$ left-justified rows of lengths $\lambda_i$. A Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ is a filling of the boxes of this diagram with positive integers. It is standard when its entries are $1,\dots,|\lambda|$, each used once, and increase along rows and down columns, and [semistandard](c:semistandard-young-tableau) when its entries increase weakly along rows and strictly down columns.
examples: The shape $(3,2)$ with rows $1\,2\,4$ and $3\,5$ is a standard Young tableau.
The shape $(2,2)$ with rows $1\,1$ and $2\,2$ is a semistandard Young tableau, but not a standard one, since entries repeat.
The shape $(2,1)$ with rows $5\,5$ and $5$ is a Young tableau but not semistandard, since the first column does not increase strictly.
Non-example: rows of lengths $1$ and $2$ from top to bottom do not form a Young diagram, because row lengths may not increase downward, so no tableau has this shape.

steps: Take a Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ with positive integer entries.
Require the entries to increase weakly along each row.
Require the entries to increase strictly down each column.
A tableau that meets both conditions is a semistandard Young tableau.
links.why: It shows which two conditions single out the semistandard tableaux among all fillings.

steps: Take a Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ with $n=|\lambda|$ boxes.
Require that its entries are the numbers $1,\dots,n$, each used exactly once.
Require the entries to increase along each row and down each column.
A tableau with these conditions is a standard Young tableau.
links.why: It shows which conditions single out the standard tableaux among all fillings.

reminder: In the Zariski topology on a prime spectrum, the closed sets are the sets $V(I)$ of primes that contain an ideal $I$.
definition: For a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the Zariski topology on the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) $\operatorname{Spec}R$ has as closed sets exactly the sets $V(I)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R:I\subseteq\mathfrak p\}$ for [ideals](c:ideal) $I$ of $R$, which makes $\operatorname{Spec}R$ a [topological space](c:topological-space). On affine space $k^n$ over a field $k$ the closed sets are the common zero sets of families of [polynomials](c:polynomial).
examples: On $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ the closed sets are the whole space and the finite sets of nonzero primes $(p)$.
For algebraically closed $k$, the closed subsets of $k$ are the finite sets and $k$ itself, which is the cofinite topology.
Non-example: the closed unit disc is closed in the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb{C}$, but it is not Zariski closed, since a nonzero one-variable polynomial has only finitely many zeros.

reminder: A zero-free region of an L-function is a region of the complex plane in which the function has no zeros.
definition: A zero-free region of a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) $F$, such as the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) or the [L-function](c:l-function) of a [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character), is a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ with $F(s)\ne0$ for all $s\in\Omega$. In analytic number theory one wants $\Omega$ inside the critical strip $0<\operatorname{Re}s<1$, next to the line $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ and as large as possible, for example $\sigma>1-c/\log(|t|+2)$ for $s=\sigma+it$.
examples: The half-plane $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ is zero-free for $\zeta$, because the Euler product converges there and is not zero.
The classical region $\sigma\ge1-c/\log(|t|+2)$ for a constant $c>0$ is zero-free for $\zeta(s)$ (de la Vallee Poussin).
Non-example: the strip $0<\sigma<1$ is not zero-free for $\zeta$, since $\zeta$ has zeros on the line $\sigma=\frac12$, the first at $t\approx14.13$.
